title: Pinterest's Idea Pins — Picking the Feature's Success Metric
scenario_context: Pinterest ships Idea Pins, a short-video format for step-by-step ideas like recipes and DIY projects. The team's stated goal is to help users discover ideas they actually intend to come back to and try, not simply to get people watching more video.
description: Which is the best primary success metric for this launch?
options: Average watch time per Idea Pin view, since a longer watch means the content held their attention.
The share of Idea Pin views that end with the viewer saving the Pin to one of their boards.
Total number of Idea Pins published by creators on the platform that month.
The number of new boards created platform-wide that month, since boards are where saved ideas live.
explanation: Option B is correct: saving a Pin is the concrete, trackable action that maps directly to 'intend to come back to this and try it' — it's scoped to the exact viewer behavior the goal describes. Option A mistakes attention for intent; a viewer can watch an entire Idea Pin passively, hooked by the video, without ever planning to act on what they saw. Option C measures the creator side of the platform, not whether viewers found anything worth acting on — supply volume can rise with no change in viewer value at all. Option D is too indirect: a new board can be created for any reason unrelated to this feature, and a saved idea doesn't require a new board at all — most saves land in a board the viewer already has.
hints: Ask which of these four options describes something the viewer actively decides to do, rather than something that happens passively while a video plays, or something creators are doing on the other side of the platform.
The stated goal is about intending to come back to an idea later — look for the option that maps to the one action already built for storing something to revisit.

title: Snapchat's Notification-Triggered Opens — What Does DAU Miss?
scenario_context: A Snapchat user gets a push notification with a red badge count whenever a friend sends a new Snap. Most days, the user taps the notification, the Snap plays for under a second, and they back out without opening anything else in the app.
description: Under a standard 'opened the app that day' DAU definition, what does this pattern reveal?
options: It shows nothing unusual — any registered app open is a meaningful signal of product value by definition, regardless of session length.
It shows the notification system itself is broken, since a well-designed badge should never be dismissed without the user reading the content.
It shows DAU should be replaced entirely by session length, since duration alone determines whether engagement is genuine.
It shows DAU can rise from a reflexive notification-clear, not real engagement — the definition doesn't distinguish the two.
explanation: Option D is correct: a standard DAU definition only requires that the app was opened that day — it doesn't ask why. A notification-triggered, sub-one-second open counts exactly the same as a genuine session, so DAU can rise purely from badge-clearing behavior with no real engagement behind it. Option A denies the premise outright, treating every registered open as automatically meaningful, which is the exact assumption this pattern breaks. Option B misdiagnoses the issue as a notification-system defect; nothing is malfunctioning here — the badge worked as designed, it's the metric that's failing to distinguish reflex from intent. Option C overcorrects into replacing DAU with session length alone, but duration has its own blind spots (an idle backgrounded app can log long 'session' time with zero engagement), so it isn't a clean substitute either.
hints: Ask what the standard 'opened the app' DAU definition actually requires the user to have done — and what it does NOT require.
The trigger for this open was a badge count, not the user seeking out content on their own — think about what that means for what DAU is actually measuring here.

title: Grubhub's Cart-to-Order Rate — Catching the Analyst's Wrong Denominator
scenario_context: Grubhub's restaurant-search funnel this week: 250,000 restaurant searches, 90,000 restaurant page views, 36,000 carts with at least one item added, and 25,200 orders placed. A junior analyst is asked to report the conversion rate specifically for the 'added an item to cart' to 'order placed' step, and writes: '28%, calculated as 25,200 orders divided by 90,000 restaurant page views.'
description: What's the flaw in the analyst's calculation?
options: The analyst used total page views (90,000) as the denominator, instead of the 36,000 carts that actually entered this step.
The calculation is correct — 90,000 is the right denominator, since it represents everyone who could have gone on to order.
The flaw is the numerator, not the denominator — total searches (250,000) should replace orders placed in the calculation.
The math has no flaw, but 28% is too low to be believable for this step, so the event-tracking data must be broken.
explanation: Option A is correct: the step being asked about starts at 'added an item to cart,' so the denominator must be the population that entered that exact step — the 36,000 carts — not the 90,000 page views from one stage earlier. Using the right denominator: 25,200 / 36,000 = 70%, a very different picture from the reported 28%. Option B defends the wrong denominator; 90,000 is the population for an earlier step (page view to cart), and plenty of those viewers never added anything to a cart, so they were never part of this step's population. Option C misdiagnoses where the error is — the numerator (25,200 orders placed) is exactly right for this step; only the denominator was wrong. Option D assumes the number itself is too implausible to trust and blames the data, but nothing here points to broken tracking — the arithmetic fully explains the low figure as a straightforward denominator mistake.
hints: Before judging the percentage itself, check which population actually entered the step being asked about — is it the same population the analyst used in the calculation?
A step's conversion rate denominator should always be the group that entered THAT step, not a stage further upstream in the funnel.

title: Reddit's 'Flat' Comment Rate — One Number, Two Opposite Stories?
scenario_context: Reddit's platform-wide average comments-per-post has held roughly flat, 8.3 this month versus 8.4 last month. A PM tells leadership: 'engagement is stable, nothing to investigate.' A data scientist breaks the same metric down by community age and finds a different story underneath: on subreddits created in the last 6 months, comments-per-post rose from 3.0 to 5.5; on subreddits older than 6 months, comments-per-post fell from 9.6 to 8.7. Posting volume has also been shifting toward the newer subreddits over the same period.
description: What's the most defensible read of this pattern?
options: The roughly-flat aggregate is coincidental — comments-per-post genuinely rose in newer subreddits and genuinely fell in older ones, and 8.3 is just what a rising number and a falling number look like averaged together; both trends deserve their own investigation.

The pattern is fully explained by posting volume shifting toward newer subreddits — since that segment naturally has fewer comments per post, the mix change alone would produce a roughly flat headline number with no real change in either community's own behavior.

The declining older-subreddit number (9.6 to 8.7) is the one signal worth acting on, since established communities still carry most of the platform's comment volume and the newer-subreddit segment is too small today to prioritize.

This is most likely ordinary month-to-month noise in both segments; with only one month of data, the roughly-flat platform-wide number is the more stable read to trust until a longer trend confirms otherwise.
explanation: Option A is correct: a platform-wide number that barely moves can still be the product of two real, opposite-direction movements happening underneath it — comments-per-post rose about 83% in newer subreddits (3.0 to 5.5) and fell about 9% in older ones (9.6 to 8.7), and a roughly-flat 8.3 is consistent with those two genuine trends landing close to each other in the aggregate, not with 'nothing happening.' Both movements are large enough, and specific enough, to warrant their own investigation rather than being waved away by the flat topline. Option B assumes the mix-shift alone explains the pattern, but that would only be true if neither segment's own number had actually moved — here both segments moved substantially on their own, so 'it's just a reweighting of the same two numbers' doesn't hold; something real changed inside each segment. Option C prioritizes the older-subreddit decline purely because that segment is larger today, but it dismisses a newer-subreddit segment that is both improving and growing its share of posts — exactly the kind of leading indicator worth tracking in its own right, not a rounding error. Option D's 'probably noise' framing doesn't fit the specificity of the pattern: two segments moving by double-digit percentages in opposite directions in the same month, alongside a real shift in posting mix, is a coherent story, not the kind of thing a single month of randomness typically produces.
hints: Before accepting 'roughly flat means stable,' ask whether the same near-flat number could be produced by two different things happening underneath it at once.
Compare how much each community-age segment's own number moved on its own, not just how the mix between segments is shifting, before deciding what the flat aggregate is telling you.

title: Twitch's Big-Streamer Feed — Session Lift, Retention Down: Which Read Wins?
scenario_context: Twitch tests a change to its 'Recommended for you' row that shows only currently-live channels with 10,000+ concurrent viewers, replacing a mix that also surfaced smaller live streamers. The test runs for a full quarter. Looking only at viewers who first joined Twitch during the test's opening week — old enough by quarter's end to have a full 90-day retention read — average watch-time per session over the quarter is up 14% in the treatment group versus control, but 90-day retention for that same cohort is down 5 percentage points versus control.
description: What's the most defensible read of this result?
options: Ship it — watch-time per session is the more statistically robust number, since it's measured across every session in the quarter, not just one cohort's 90-day read.
Treat this as a wash: the session-level lift and the retention drop are roughly comparable in size, so the result nets out to neutral — test a different idea instead.
This is a genuine trade-off: retention is the load-bearing signal, since large-streamer picks can lift a session's watch-time without building the loyalty that brings a viewer back.
Revert this immediately: any test where a retention metric moves the wrong way should be killed regardless of what else moved, since retention is Twitch's single most important number.
explanation: Option C is correct: this is a genuine short-term-lift-versus-long-term-retention trade-off, and retention is the metric that should carry more weight here, not because it's labeled more important but because of the mechanism behind each number. A large, currently-live streamer is inherently easy to enjoy for a single session — production value, a big moment — without a new viewer ever forming the channel loyalty that usually brings someone back to Twitch specifically over the following months. A session-level lift that comes from removing exactly that discovery pathway looks like borrowing future engagement, not creating it. Option A treats 'measured across more sessions' as equivalent to 'matters more for this decision' — a larger sample makes a number more precise, but precision doesn't make session-level watch-time a better proxy for durable platform health than a cohort's actual 90-day return behavior. Option B treats a percentage change in one metric and a percentage-point change in a different metric as comparable, offsetting quantities, but they're different units measuring different things; one can't be netted against the other to call the result neutral. Option D elevates retention to an automatic veto without weighing why it moved or by how much relative to the session gain — treating any retention dip as instantly disqualifying would block nearly every discovery-surface experiment, since some near-term-versus-long-term tension is common. The defensible move is weighing the trade-off, which is what Option C does and Option D skips.
hints: Ask what would make a viewer stick around for months, versus what would just make one session more watchable in the moment — are those driven by the same thing here?

A percentage change in one metric and a percentage-point change in a different metric aren't automatically comparable just because both moved — think about what each one actually measures before weighing them against each other.

title: Figma's Weekly Actives — Editors Only, or Everyone Who Opened a File?
scenario_context: Figma currently defines Weekly Active Users as anyone who edited a design file that week: 1.2 million by that definition. A PM proposes broadening the definition to anyone who opened OR commented on a file that week, even without editing, arguing viewers and commenters are 'still using the product.' Under the broader definition, WAU is 3.8 million. The PM wants to switch to reporting 3.8 million to the board starting this quarter, without restating prior quarters under the new definition.
description: What's the strongest critique of the PM's proposal?
options: None — view-only and comment-only users are still real usage of the product, and a broader definition that captures more of Figma's actual audience is a more complete picture of engagement.
The two figures measure different populations, creators versus passive viewers, and switching this quarter without restating prior quarters breaks every trend comparison the board has seen.
The real issue is reporting cadence, not definition — Figma should switch from Weekly Active Users to Daily Active Users, since a daily figure would resolve the editor-versus-viewer ambiguity.
Both figures are equally legitimate ways to measure activity, so the choice should come down to whichever number the board responds to better this quarter.
explanation: Option B is correct: 'edited a file' and 'opened or commented on a file' aren't the same behavior measured at two thresholds, they're two different populations — one is people actively creating design work, the other includes people who never touched a canvas. Reporting 3.8 million this quarter without restating prior quarters under the same broader definition means the board can no longer compare this number to anything they've seen before; the next quarter-over-quarter read would be measuring a definition change, not a business change. Option A treats 'more inclusive' as automatically better, but the question isn't whether viewer activity has any value at all — it's whether folding a fundamentally different behavior into the same number as design creation, mid-stream and without restating history, still lets the metric mean what the board thinks it means. Option C reaches for a different axis of the metric, the reporting window, that has nothing to do with the actual problem — swapping WAU for DAU would still face the identical editor-versus-viewer ambiguity, just measured daily instead of weekly. Option D treats this as a matter of which number lands better with the board, sidestepping that the two definitions measure genuinely different things and that switching without restating history breaks every trend comparison going forward, regardless of which number is preferred.
hints: Ask whether 'edited a file' and 'opened or commented on a file' are really the same behavior measured at two thresholds, or two different things entirely.
Think about what happens to every quarter-over-quarter comparison the board has ever seen if the definition changes starting this quarter without restating the earlier numbers.

title: Poshmark's Posh Ambassador badge — designing a threshold a share-bot can't clear
scenario_context: Poshmark's 'Posh Ambassador' badge grants a search-visibility boost to sellers who meet daily activity thresholds. The current qualifying metric is items shared per day — sellers can share their own or others' listings to their followers, Poshmark's core social mechanic. Growth has found sellers running third-party bot tools that auto-share hundreds of stale, unsold listings a day purely to keep the badge, with no real shop activity behind it. The team is redesigning the formula to survive a seller actively trying to keep the badge without running a healthy shop.
description: Which candidate qualifying formula is most robust against that kind of gaming?
options: Total items shared per day, unchanged, since sharing is Poshmark's core community mechanic and reflects genuine engagement.
Total items shared per day, but require shares to spread across at least 20 distinct minutes, filtering out mass-sharing sessions.
A blend of items sold per month, average days-to-sale, and shares capped at a modest daily ceiling so volume stops adding value.
Total number of Poshmark followers, since more followers reflects a larger, more engaged community built over time.
explanation: Option C is correct: it ties the badge to outcomes a bot campaign cannot manufacture, items actually sold and how quickly a seller's own inventory moves, while capping the one lever a script can pull for free, share volume, so pushing shares past the ceiling stops helping at all. A seller who wants the badge now has to run a shop that actually sells and stays fresh, not just fire off shares all day. Option A leaves the exact vulnerability untouched: share count is entirely within a seller's control, including via automation, so nothing about the gaming strategy changes. Option B's minute-spacing rule sounds like a real technical countermeasure, but it only raises the bar for how a bot is configured, spacing automated shares across the day is a trivial adjustment for anyone already running a share bot, not a genuine behavioral requirement. Option D rewards accumulated follower count, a number that only grows and is itself purchasable or gameable through follow-for-follow schemes, and it says nothing about whether a seller is currently running a healthy, active shop.
hints: Ask what a seller could script or automate for free, at scale, purely to hit the threshold — and whether each candidate still rewards that.
A qualifying metric resists gaming when it requires something a bot can't fake: an independent buyer actually completing a purchase.

title: YouTube Kids' high-energy recommendation lift — is more watch time actually the win?
scenario_context: YouTube Kids tests a recommendation change that raises average watch time per session by 20% by surfacing more 'high-energy' content — bright colors, fast cuts, unpredictable rewards — a format style correlated with longer sessions industry-wide. The company's own child-development advisors flag that this content pattern is associated in published research with attention and self-regulation difficulties in young children, though no causal study has been run on YouTube Kids' own users specifically. Leadership must decide whether to ship the change broadly.
description: Given the tension between a strong engagement number and what's driving it, what's the most defensible strategic call?
options: Ship broadly — a 20% watch-time lift is a meaningful win, and advisor concern without a product-specific study isn't reason enough to withhold it.
Redefine success before shipping broadly — pair the watch-time metric with a guardrail capping high-energy content's share of what gets surfaced.
Commission a full causal study on YouTube Kids' own users first, and treat the watch-time lift as inconclusive until it reports back.
Ship broadly, but add a parental control letting parents cap daily watch time, treating that as sufficient mitigation on its own.
explanation: Option B is correct: in a children's product, 'more watch time' isn't automatically success — the goal-metric tension here is that the specific mechanism driving the lift, more high-energy, unpredictable-reward content, is the exact content pattern the company's own child-development advisors associate with attention and self-regulation risk in this audience. That doesn't require a completed causal study on YouTube Kids specifically to act on responsibly; it requires redefining what this launch's success means so that watch time is paired with a guardrail on content composition, not treated as a stand-alone win. That's the strategic, portfolio-health-level judgment: protect the thing the product actually owes its youngest users before crediting a raw engagement number. Option A treats a 20% lift as sufficient justification on its own and demands a completed, product-specific causal study as the only bar for caution, but waiting for perfect, product-specific proof before acting on a well-supported directional concern from the company's own advisors is exactly the failure mode a strategic health lens exists to catch. Option C swings to full paralysis, a year-plus wait with no interim constraint, which both delays legitimate product improvement and does nothing to limit exposure to the flagged content pattern in the meantime; a defensible interim guardrail doesn't require the study to already be finished. Option D adds a real feature, but a parental time cap is opt-in and reactive, most parents never discover or configure it, and it doesn't address the underlying question of whether the algorithm itself should be surfacing more of this specific content pattern, a structural question a settings toggle can't answer for a family that never touches it.
hints: Ask what specifically is driving the watch-time increase, not just whether the number itself went up — the mechanism matters as much as the metric here.
The question isn't whether to prove harm before ever acting — it's what a responsible interim definition of success looks like while evidence is still incomplete.

title: Carvana's Instant Approval flow — three signals, one verdict
scenario_context: Carvana tests an 'Instant Approval' financing flow that shows a provisional loan approval and payment estimate right after basic info entry, before the hard credit pull, aiming to raise checkout starts. Three-week test: checkout starts are up 26% in week 1 but down to 11% by week 3. The guardrail, the rate of users shown an instant approval who are then denied after the real credit pull, is up from 4% to 13% specifically on Instant-Approval checkouts. A segment cut shows the checkout-start lift is concentrated entirely among new customers with no prior credit history in Carvana's system; returning customers with an existing approved-financing history show no meaningful change.
description: Given all three signals together, what's the most defensible call?
options: Ship to 100% — even an 11% week-3 lift is real, and a rising denial-after-approval rate is a normal part of any pre-qualification flow.
Kill the feature outright and never retest in any form — a rising denial-after-approval rate is disqualifying on principle in a financial product.
Ship only to new customers with no prior credit history, and address the denial-rate guardrail later once there's more usage data to tune against.
Hold the rollout and don't extend as-is — tighten the pre-qualification model before testing again, given all three signals together.
explanation: Option D is correct: three signals are compounding, and their combination is what makes this a hold, not a ship. The checkout-start lift is fading fast, a classic novelty signature, the benefit that remains is concentrated in one segment, new customers, not a broad win across the base, and the guardrail moving the wrong way is measuring the exact promise this feature makes, an instant approval that then gets reversed after the real credit check. In a financial product, telling a customer they're approved and then denying them at the final step isn't a side cost to weigh against conversion, it's evidence the pre-qualification model isn't accurate enough yet, and every reversal is a trust hit precisely to the new-customer segment the feature is supposed to be winning over. The defensible next step is tightening the pre-qualification logic so 'instant approval' means something closer to what it promises, then testing again, not extending or shipping this version. Option A treats the rising denial-after-approval rate as an unremarkable part of any pre-qualification flow, but this isn't a soft, private pre-qualification, it's a customer-facing promise that gets broken at checkout, a materially different and more damaging pattern than a typical soft-check false positive. Option B jumps to a permanent, no-retest kill, foreclosing the possibility that a more accurate pre-qualification model could deliver the same checkout-start benefit without the broken-promise pattern, a bigger commitment than the evidence calls for. Option C reapplies a segmentation-only fix, but it explicitly defers the guardrail 'until more usage data,' which means knowingly continuing to tell new customers, exactly the segment both driving the lift and bearing the rising denial rate, that they're approved when a meaningful and growing share of them aren't.
hints: Three different signals moved here. Before treating any one of them as decisive on its own, ask what story they tell together.
One of these signals is measuring whether the feature's core promise to the customer actually holds up. Weigh what a rising version of that signal means for trust, not just for the funnel.
